name: Septal extension graft
lead: A septal extension graft is a piece of cartilage, usually from the septum, attached to the end of the nasal septum in rhinoplasty to control the position, length, projection and rotation of the nasal tip. It is used particularly in patients with weak lower lateral cartilages.[1][2]

For appearance, it lets a surgeon set how far the tip of the nose sticks out, how much it points upward and how long the nose looks from the side. Patients with a droopy, underprojected or short nose use it to get a longer, more rotated and better-supported tip, and the graft also steadies the tip against changes during healing.[1][2][3]

In looksmaxxing discussion it is associated with lengthening or rotating the nose tip. The evidence is surgical case series, comparative cohort studies, randomised comparisons with the columellar strut graft and several registered trials.

paras: A 1997 paper identified methods for controlling nasal tip position and shape in patients at risk of losing projection, whose noses showed a weak midvault, a plunging tip with a "Polly beak" and drawn-up alae, and reported on septal extension grafts in 20 such patients.[1] A 2014 introduction in Archives of Plastic Surgery describes the graft,[3] and a 2007 paper describes a complete septal extension graft for Korean patients using an extensive harvesting technique.[4] A 2009 paper described a modified version placed through an extended marginal incision.[13]

Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article says the septal extension graft gives more tip control and changes less over time than a columellar strut.[2] The graft is typically placed during open rhinoplasty, where the surgeon has direct view of the tip cartilages.[2] Cartilage usually comes from the septum, and rib or ear cartilage is used when septal cartilage is not enough, as is common in revisions; synthetic materials appear when autologous grafts are unavailable.[2] A 2024 technical report examined a porous polyethylene extension graft in oriental rhinoplasty for cases where autologous cartilage is limited.[14]

The graft is applied to short or underprojected noses, droopy tips and tips with weak lower lateral cartilages.[1][2] Reports describe its use to correct an overly shortened nose, in cleft nasal deformity, in Asian rhinoplasty and in alar collapse.[15][16][17][18] A 2023 series examined it for alar collapse, a cause of nasal obstruction.[18]

Rhinoplasty itself dates to ancient reconstructive work described in Egyptian and Indian texts, with the modern era beginning with John Orlando Roe's endonasal operation in 1887 and Aurel Rethi's open approach in 1934, according to Wikipedia.[2] The septal extension graft was set out as a tip-control method in the 1997 Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery paper, which has been widely cited since.[1] As open rhinoplasty became standard, grafts that build tip structure, including the columellar strut and the extension graft, became common tools.[2]

A 2014 JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery study reported complications of septal extension grafts in Asian patients.[5] Reviews of Asian rhinoplasty note that cartilage grafts carry a risk of revision surgery from issues such as warping.[6] Wikipedia describes outcomes as somewhat unpredictable because healing varies, says swelling can take a year or more to resolve, and puts overall revision rhinoplasty at roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations.[2]

A 2024 functional evaluation looked at an L-strut extension graft in East Asians, and a 2023 finite element analysis modelled how the graft affects tip support.[19][20] A rigid extension can reduce tip flexibility, which a 2024 trial of graft types addressed.[21]

A 2019 retrospective cohort compared maintenance of tip projection and rotation after columellar strut versus caudal septal extension graft, noting that no quantitative comparison existed beforehand.[7] A 2024 randomised trial in secondary cleft rhinoplasty divided 33 patients into strut and extension groups and tracked profile photographs up to 12 months,[22] a 2024 prospective trial compared tip flexibility and stability between the two,[21] and a 2026 comparative trial followed tip projection and rotation at six and 12 months.[23]

Other work includes a 2022 series on extension grafts for increased tip projection,[24] and registered trials comparing septal extension graft versus columellar strut (NCT06958575),[8] unilateral versus bilateral grafts in droopy tips (NCT07446426)[9] and a patient-reported outcomes study (NCT07531810).[10]

card.summary: A cartilage graft that extends the septum to control nose-tip length, projection and rotation; established technique with growing comparative data.
card.note: Complications have been reported in Asian patients; trials against columellar struts are ongoing.

quick.overview:
A septal extension graft attaches cartilage to the end of the septum so the surgeon can set the tip's position, length and rotation. It is used mostly for weak or underprojected tips.

Wikipedia says it gives more control and changes less than a columellar strut; a 2019 cohort compared the two.
quick.mechanism: Cartilage, usually harvested from the septum, is fixed to the caudal septum, creating a stable platform for the tip cartilages.
quick.risks: A 2014 study reported complications of the graft in Asian patients. As with other rhinoplasty, revision surgery can be needed.

chain: Cartilage graft is fixed to the end of the septum
Tip is held at a chosen length, projection and rotation
Longer, more defined and better-supported nose tip
angle.text: The graft builds a stable cartilage frame under the nose tip so the surgeon can set its position. People choose it to lengthen or rotate a short or drooping nose and to keep the result stable over time.
